extracted.intended_audience: students learning news writing / journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: Exercises and practice prompts for rewriting news-style sentences and short paragraphs to improve coherence, emphasis, diction, grammar, and idiomatic usage in journalistic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite the following sentences in any way that will improve their coherence (mainly paragraphs 163-164).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast run-on or awkwardly connected clauses so ideas flow logically; remove repeated qualifiers (e.g., multiple "fortunately"), reorder clauses so cause/effect and main points are clear, and compress or split sentences where necessary. Examples include long, repetitive disaster reports and sentences with several loosely connected clauses that should be reorganized for a clear main idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The following sentences lack emphasis. Explain why and improve the emphasis in each (paragraphs 165-168).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the important fact the focal point of the sentence (lead with the essential information), avoid burying newsworthy elements in subordinate clauses, and use sentence structure to give weight to the key point. Examples show buried subjects (e.g., "As we go to press... the news comes to us that... was instantly killed") that should be recast to foreground the main event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid crude or affected phraseology
rubrics_metrics.description: The following sentences are unemphatic because of their crude or affected phraseology. Rewrite each so that it shall be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove affected, overly ornate, or awkward turns of phrase; eliminate inflated metaphors, mixed images, and archaic constructions; favor natural, direct diction appropriate to news copy. Examples: overblown descriptions of social events, strained metaphors, and pompous sentence constructions that undermine clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fine shades of word meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the meanings of the words in the following groups (e.g., Abscond, avoid, decamp, elude...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words with the correct denotation and connotation for the context; recognize subtle differences among near-synonyms to avoid imprecise or misleading wording in news copy. Exercise lists groups of related words to practice precise selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concise equivalents to wordy phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Give equivalents for the following phrases (many are wordy clichés or roundabout expressions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace long, clumsy, or clichéd phrases (e.g., 'departed this life', 'led to the hymeneal altar') with shorter, plain-language equivalents suitable for journalistic style. This trains reducing verbosity and eliminating worn phrases that weaken copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct grammar and idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct the following sentences (numerous examples of faulty grammar, bad idiom, and awkward constructions are provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix subject-verb agreement, misplaced modifiers, faulty parallelism, incorrect participles, pronoun ambiguity, punctuation errors, and other grammatical faults so sentences read naturally and correctly. Examples include confused passive constructions, illogical sentence order, and improper word forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of expression / conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid needless words and redundant modifiers; make sentences economical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate pleonasms (unnecessary repetition), redundant qualifiers, and inflated phrasing. Many exercise sentences demonstrate verbosity (e.g., repeating 'beautiful' several times, multiple adjectives in sequence) and should be tightened to essential information for news readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and factual clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure statements are specific and factually clear rather than vague or misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace vague language and hearsay with precise facts and accurate phrasing (e.g., correct false reports, avoid implying uncertain facts as certain). Several exercises include reports of events or numbers that must be stated clearly and unambiguously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use active voice and direct phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active constructions and direct wording over passive, evasive, or roundabout phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast sentences that bury actors with passive voice or convoluted clauses into active, direct forms to increase clarity and immediacy. Examples: sentences that begin with 'As we go to press...' or use multiple nominalizations should be rewritten to state who did what.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appropriate journalistic tone / avoid melodrama
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep tone fitting for news: objective, restrained, and clear; avoid melodramatic or subjective embellishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove exaggerated adjectives, sentimental or promotional language, and overt editorializing (e.g., extravagant praise, hyperbolic decorations of events). Rewrite to report facts plainly and let significance arise from facts rather than flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange information for logical sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize sentence elements so that the logical relationships (time, cause, contrast) are obvious to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place modifiers next to the words they modify, order clauses to reflect chronology or causation, and split or join sentences to preserve coherence. The exercises show many misordered clauses and awkward sequences that should be reorganized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and stale expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace hackneyed phrases and worn metaphors with fresh, precise wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many listed phrases (chapter exercises) are traditional journalistic clichés; students are asked to supply better equivalents. Avoid overused expressions that dilute impact and make prose seem unoriginal.
